title: León XIV and the Quispe sisters, the Vatican and the communion rails, Viganò responds to Reid, Baltimore, Denver, Alessandria, Wilmer, Puebla, Nicaragua, Etchmiadzin, Amaras, Coatnet, Shalom, the exorcism of Simoni, Shenzhen, Cyril at eighty, Greta, Augias.
excerpt: Federica Tourn maintains that the trip to Peru ignored the victims’ outcry and places the Quispe sisters at the center; they filed a complaint with then-Bishop Prevost in 2022 and are still awaiting a hearing. In August the Dicastery for…
content:
Time flies, it is already Friday, the week is drawing to a close, the month of November is heading toward its end and Advent is beginning to be in the air. At this very moment a huge crane, as tall as the obelisk, is hoisting the Christmas tree into place and the Nativity scene continues its assembly. Roman autumns are wonderful; today we have a sunny morning that invites one to wander through the streets of Rome. We move on to another day that does not disappoint: we continue with the abuses in Peru and with the ignored cry of the victims of abuse, placing at the center the Quispe sisters, who reported the matter to then-Bishop Prevost in 2022 and who still have not been granted an audience. On the liturgical side, the day is marked not by a declaration but by a three-page letter that someone has made public. The traditionalist world has responded as one to the “not for now” from the plane. In Baltimore the American bishops voted on the lectionary and the secretary; in Rome the Pope received Caritas Internationalis and the Shalom community. In Shenzhen three powers signed a peace agreement in which the Church does not appear, and the Patriarch of Moscow turns eighty today. A dense day with many proper names; let us begin.

The Quispe sisters still have no audience

Federica Tourn reports today that the trip to Peru ignored the cry of the victims of abuse, and the case she places at the center is the one that touches the Pope most closely: that of Ana-María Quispe and her two younger sisters, who denounced two priests of Chiclayo for abuses suffered as girls and who have been requesting an audience with Prevost for years without success. The chronology must be read carefully. On 5 April 2022 they reported Eleuterio “Lute” Vásquez Gonzáles—whose whereabouts are unknown—and Ricardo Yesquén to then-Bishop Prevost. On 21 July 2022, according to the diocese, the file was sent to the Holy See, although the sisters maintain that no investigation took place that year and that the diocese let nineteen months pass. On 3 July 2023 the diocese transferred the civil-case file, and on 10 August the Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith archived the case. In November 2025 Lute received from Prevost a dispensatio ab oneribus, the dispensation from the clerical state, of which the sisters learned informally.

The rest of the picture fits with what we have been reporting for ten days. Escardó, one of the first to denounce the Sodalicio—founded by Luis Fernando Figari in 1971 and dissolved in April 2025—maintains that no victim of the Sodalicio was invited to the nunciature in Lima and points to the president of the Peruvian Episcopal Conference and the nuncio, a claim the president denies; Jordi Bertomeu says he suggested criteria and names but that the final decision was taken by other Vatican instances, as he already recounted on Tuesday. The Survivors’ Network of Peru demonstrated outside the nunciature, and BishopAccountability, SNAP and Ending Clergy Abuse called for transparency, justice and reparation. Anne Barrett Doyle leaves the two sentences that headline the story: “the Pope has not responded to our letter,” and “we fear that Robert Prevost, as he has become more powerful, has also become more cautious.” The piece itself warns that the diocese and Vatican sources dispute part of the account, and we report that. What is not in dispute are the dates, and what is not in dispute is that the victims he knows by name and surname were not included in the selection of the eleven.

The Vatican upholds the Bishop of Charlotte, and the signature is Viola’s

Messa in Latino publishes the letter: three pages, protocol 482/26, dated 3 August 2026, by which the Dicastery for Divine Worship and the Discipline of the Sacraments rejects the hierarchical recourse against the norms of Bishop Michael Martin of Charlotte, which prohibit the use of the communion rail, kneelers and prie-dieux for distributing Communion. The recourse was filed on 20 June by a father of a family who says he was repeatedly denied Communion in the parish of Our Lady of Grace in Greensboro for kneeling at the rail, together with his wife and two children. The response argues that the bishop, as “moderator, promoter and guardian of liturgical life,” may regulate the external modalities of distribution under canons 381 §1 and 838 §4, that the diocesan norms do not deny access to the sacrament nor prohibit receiving Communion on one’s knees, and that denial would occur only if a faithful person who presents himself in the prescribed manner were refused Communion solely for kneeling. The sentence that sustains everything: “every faithful person retains the right to receive Holy Communion,” but “there is no corresponding subjective right to demand” that it be distributed with a particular piece of furniture.

The dates matter. Martin’s norms come from a pastoral letter of 17 December 2025, in force since 16 January; in January thirty-one diocesan priests, about a quarter of the clergy, presented a dubia to the Dicastery for Legislative Texts on the bishop’s authority to prohibit kneelers and rails, and no response to that dubia is known. What we had not noticed until today is who signed the August letter: Archbishop Vittorio Francesco Viola, then secretary of the dicastery, that is, the same man the Pope welcomed the day before yesterday as archpriest of St. Peter’s, in the paragraph of the centenary homily we reported yesterday. The new archpriest of the basilica is the one who signed that there is no right to receive Communion at the communion rails.

Radio Spada gives the same data—the recourse of 20 June addressed to Cardinal Roche, the response of 3 August signed by Viola, the publication by AdVaticanum on 18 November—and adds its own reading, that of moderate disobedience: that resorting to the present tribunals is equivalent to accepting that a right can be denied. Messa in Latino, for its part, points out two procedural matters worth noting: that the family has sixty days to appeal to the Apostolic Signatura from formal notification, and ten days to ask the dicastery itself to review its decision.

Viganò replies to Dom Alcuin Reid

Aldo Maria Valli publishes in Duc in altum a text signed by Viganò, dated 18 November, that responds to the open letter of Dom Alcuin Reid we reported yesterday. He grants two points: that the consultation of the bishops did not say what the motu proprio claims, and that unity is not uniformity. He reproaches the rest, beginning with the tone: that a scholar should have been more rigorous, that flattery of the Pope is out of place, and that criticizing the “ideology” of the bishops before a Pope who shares it leads nowhere. His fundamental argument is one of law, not of grace: the Mass of St. Pius V does not need permission because Quo primum grants it in perpetuity; calling it a “concession” implicitly accepts that it can be revoked, and that is the principle applied by Traditionis custodes. The phrase is good and is his: “a favor is withdrawn, a right is not.” The conclusion is the usual one: he asks that the motu proprio be abrogated as an act of justice and only together with the condemnation of the errors that inspired it, and he closes with “frequent the Mass of all time, even when the pastors forbid it to you.” With this the map of the week is complete: Reid asks to be heard, Viglione announces the underground, the Wanderer waits, and Viganò denies that there is anything to ask for.

The “not for now” and what the transcript says

And here is a verifiable datum that deserves attention. Sabino Paciolla translates a comment from Rorate Caeli that maintains the official transcript of the flight cut the Pope’s answer: that he said “no, non in questo momento” and that the published text leaves it as a plain “no”. From there comes the headline the Italian blog puts in the mouth of the English medium, and it is his, not the Pope’s: that Catholics attached to the traditional rites will continue to be “second-class citizens within the Church.” The article also records a practical observation by Diane Montagna that does have consequences: that in February 2022 the dicastery of Roche obliged bishops to give prior notice before granting dispensations, by means of a rescript of Pope Francis, and that that rescript could be revoked without touching the motu proprio, returning the faculty to the local bishops.

LifeSiteNews, with the by-line of Antonino Cambria, tallies the reactions and headlines that no one has been surprised: Joseph Shaw of Una Voce International calls it disappointing but maintains that it leaves an “enormous” margin and applies Michael Davies’s test—what does this permit that was not permitted before; the Arlington Latin Mass Society prays “every day” for abrogation and clings to the “no, for now” and the path of dispensation; Taylor Marshall dismisses it as “continuity candidate”; and Matt Gaspers calls for maintaining that no Pope can abolish the rites received and approved.

De Mattei gives the trip a pass, and the Wanderer retracts

Messa in Latino reproduces Roberto de Mattei’s first assessment of Argentina, and it is a favorable one: he highlights that before Milei, the authorities and the diplomatic corps the Pope insisted on the Christian heritage of the country, on the family as “the fundamental cell of society” and on the defense of life “from the first moments until its natural end”; that in Córdoba he proposed Cura Brochero and Mama Antula and presented the crucifix and the rosary as weapons of evangelization; that he warned the clergy against activism without prayer and against excusing evil with pastoral reasons; and that at the vigil he used the three youths in the furnace of Nebuchadnezzar against the idols of success, money, appearance and pleasure. He reports two million in Luján and seven million in three days according to official figures. Wanderer admits that its pessimistic forecasts failed and describes the visit as “clearly apostolic,” with the coda that speaking of Christ, conversion and eternal life are “things that do not interest politicians.” Of Wanderer we reported yesterday its thesis of resignification; today we must also note its retraction. And De Mattei underlines the reformulation of “todos, todos, todos” into “todos hacia Cristo, todos con Cristo, todos como Cristo,” which he links to the instaurare omnia in Christo of Pius X.

The primacy of mission

Michele Brambilla reads the Wednesday catechesis and is left with one idea: that the Pope uses the three slogans of the trip to ask Catholics to return to evangelizing those beside them, whatever their condition. From Uruguay he draws that a small community that takes the missionary mandate seriously can awaken an entire country; from the Argentine slogan, that fraternal dialogue and mission are not opposed; from Peru, that the witness of Toribio de Mogrovejo and Rosa of Lima is what builds the “civilization of love.” He quotes the Pope’s expression “a wholly missionary Church, which finds its coherence and its joy in evangelizing,” and recalls that the liturgical year closes with Christ the King on 22 November and that Advent begins on the 29th.

Chiclayo and synodality, one week later

This is from 13 November and is circulating again now, which says something about the text itself. In the sanctuary of Our Lady of Peace, before bishops, priests, religious, seminarians, synodal teams and pastoral councils, the Pope said that “it is easy to speak of synodality, but practicing it is a challenge,” and that this requires everyone, beginning with the pastors, to review attitudes and behaviors. The phrase that everyone has headlined is the other one: “the participation of the laity is not a concession, but an expression of their baptismal dignity.” And the foundation he places beneath it is baptism: “before any service, charge, profession or ministry, we are baptized.”

Il Nuovo Giornale Nazionale reproduces it in full, and Interris focuses on the pastoral councils, which is where the substance lies: the Pope acknowledges that their vote is only consultative and maintains that their “ecclesial importance is notable,” and asks that every community be able to constitute its own with members who commit themselves to formation. In other words, the same thing the Wanderer read yesterday as an emptying of synodality—the councils advise and the pastors decide—the Pope says exactly that and presents it as strengthening.

Baltimore: Rhoades, the lectionary and an eighteen-year cause

The autumn assembly of the bishops of the United States was held in Baltimore from 16 to 19 November and voted on much: the new Lectionary for Mass and the Book of Gospels passed 196 to 5 with 3 abstentions; a day of prayer for racial justice was instituted on the last Sunday of October, 180 to 15 with 7; the non-binding guidelines on diocesan financial information were updated, 205 to 2 with 1, and those on socially responsible investment, 217 to 0 with 1; and the 2027 budget passed 212 to 2 with 3. Bishop Oscar Cantú reported on the working group on human dignity and artificial intelligence, and Bishop Brendan Cahill on the special message on immigration published a year ago.

The election figures are the ones that count: on Tuesday the 17th, Kevin C. Rhoades, Bishop of Fort Wayne-South Bend, was re-elected secretary by 157 votes against 59 for Earl K. Fernandes, Bishop of Columbus. Rhoades had been elected in November 2025 by 126 to 95 to complete Coakley’s term; now he begins his own three-year term and will also chair the Priorities and Programs committee. Fernandes loses his second election in two years. The six commission presidencies, with mandate from November 2027, were decided as follows: Education for James Conley, 113 to 107; Pro-Life Activities for Donald Hying, 113 to 104; Doctrine for William Joensen, 115 to 104; Communications for Louis Tylka, 115 to 102; Cultural Diversity for Michael Pham, 123 to 96; and National Collections for Gerald Vincke, 127 to 86. Two by fewer than ten votes. And Paul B. R. Hartmann, priest of Milwaukee and associate general secretary since 2022, is the new general secretary from 5 December, for five years, replacing Michael Fuller.

The other decision of the assembly is a cause of canonization, and the story is what it is. The bishops, consulted by Thomas Paprocki and Archbishop Nelson Pérez, approved the opening of the diocesan phase of the cause of Maria Middleton, a laywoman of Philadelphia born on 10 September 2002 in Doylestown, whom her parents consecrated to the Virgin at baptism. At sixteen, in January 2019, she was diagnosed with an inoperable tumor in the brain stem and given nine to twelve months; she died on 8 October 2020, at eighteen. She organized coat drives and an annual collection now called Hope-A-Thon, and wrote to Archbishop Pérez during the pandemic to ask for Communion; he offered to bring it to her in person. The five-year period expired in October 2025 and the formal petition arrived in June. Pérez may now request the nihil obstat from the Dicastery for the Causes of Saints, and once the diocesan process opens she would become a Servant of God.

Denver: another pastor on “sabbatical” after Ripperger

Archbishop James Golka of Denver, appointed by Leo XIV this year, has placed Father Daniel Ciucci, pastor of Most Precious Blood, on “sabbatical” following complaints from parishioners and a signed petition. Ciucci himself recounted it in a video and a letter: it begins after Christmas, lasts about six months, ends in July and afterward he could be assigned to another parish; he describes it as a time of prayer, renewal and “examination” of his priesthood, and thanks the archbishop. The petition, on Change.org, gathered 889 signatures and was presented in 2025 to then-Archbishop Samuel Aquila: it alleged a drop in attendance at the parish and the school, staff turnover, poor morale and a unilateral style of governance. To the Denver Post, critics reproach him for preaching centered on penance, guilt and hell. In October the same archbishop imposed on the exorcist Chad Ripperger a one-year “fast” from all public ministry. There is no official explanation from the archdiocese on either case.

Alessandria: what Gallese’s accounts say

The “spese pazze” of the Bishop of Alessandria, Guido Gallese, are phantoms; the two properties at the center of the scandal enriched the diocese, and we have the figures from the dossier of the Dicastery for Bishops: the former Capuchin complex—convent, sanctuary of the Sacred Heart, theater and a dining hall that serves about one hundred fifty dinners a day—was purchased for about one hundred fifty thousand euros and is valued at nearly two million; there are three and a half million euros in public funds allocated to restoration, of which more than two million were committed by decree in June 2024; and the Collegio Santa Chiara, which cost ninety thousand euros a year when closed, now houses forty students and closes its accounts with a surplus. The apostolic visitation was entrusted to Cardinal Giuseppe Bertello and exploded in the press in January. The journalistic narrative was “built” on those two properties.

Wilmer and fornication, according to who tells it

Gaudium Press, with the by-line of Saul Castilblanco Mosos, headlines that the president of the German episcopate says that fornication is no longer condemned. What Bishop Heiner Wilmer of Münster said on Katholisch.de is that he was pleasantly surprised by the discussion on cohabitation “beyond” marriage at the meeting of presidents of episcopal conferences held in Rome in October on Amoris laetitia; that from the perspective of the Catechism the Church looks very critically on those forms of life; and that there was “great unanimity” that another language is needed, one that says “we do not condemn this, but we accompany you on the path to marriage.” On Communion for the divorced and remarried he said that opinions diverged and that the final text is not yet available. That fornication is no longer condemned is the interpretation of the medium; the quotation of number 2353 of the Catechism is supplied by the article, not by the bishop. Wilmer has presided over the German conference since 24 February, and from the same interview comes the most interesting datum: he says that conversations with Rome on the synodal path remain open, that he trusts there will be no “stop sign” and that there will be no special German regulations.

Puebla installs a new archbishop

Jorge Carlos Patrón Wong took possession on Thursday the 19th as the ninth Archbishop of Puebla de los Ángeles, at midday in the square of the Palafoxian Seminary, where the bull was read and Víctor Sánchez Espinosa handed him the crozier of Blessed Juan de Palafox y Mendoza. Leo XIV appointed him on 21 September. Born in Mérida in 1958 and a priest since 1988, he was rector of the seminary of Yucatán from 2000 to 2009 and, above all, secretary for seminaries in the then Congregation for the Clergy from 2013 to 2021, before Xalapa. The diocese he receives has enviable numbers: three hundred sixty parishes and quasi-parishes, four hundred twenty diocesan priests and one hundred ninety-eight seminarians.

His program can be seen coming from his curriculum: he proposed the motto “With Mary, all missionary disciples of Jesus Christ,” anchored it in Magnifica humanitas, in Evangelii gaudium and in Aparecida, listed five verbs—sow, accompany, educate, form, discern—as dynamics of a vocational culture, and asked that from now on prayers for vocations be said before every blessing throughout the archdiocese, because “Puebla can give many more vocations.” He named the wounds of the region—poverty, violence, corruption, injustice and loneliness—and asked for respect for life from conception to natural death. And he ratified the ministries of all the priests, which is the way of saying there will be no purge.

Nicaragua: the Pope seeks mechanisms

Bishop Carlos Herrera of Jinotega and former president of the Nicaraguan Episcopal Conference, expelled from the country in 2024, tells Artículo 66 that Leo XIV raised with him in a recent conversation the situation of the Nicaraguan Church, and that the Holy See “is seeking mechanisms” to open a dialogue with the government of Daniel Ortega and Rosario Murillo that has not been possible until now. He spoke from Costa Rica, at the assembly of the Central American Episcopal Secretariat. He gives no details of any démarche, and four Nicaraguan bishops live outside their country. The other datum from the interview concerns internal governance and has an edge: the presidency of the conference has passed to Bishop Jorge Solórzano until the end of the mandate in 2027, and Herrera says he was neither consulted nor informed, neither by the bishop who is in Nicaragua nor by the Holy See. “I have not been consulted nor informed,” and he remains waiting to see what happens.

Gugerotti, Etchmiadzin and the Catholicos

According to the Armenian Patriarchate of Jerusalem, Cardinal Claudio Gugerotti, prefect of the Dicastery for Eastern Churches, expressed on 17 November, in the Basilica of the Holy Sepulchre and before Bishop Theodoros Zakaryan, his concern over the tensions between the Armenian government and the See of Etchmiadzin and over recent actions against Catholicos Karekin II. Caution is obligatory here: the cardinal is not quoted verbatim, and the only source of his words is the account of the Patriarchate, collected through Panorama.am. Gugerotti is in the Holy Land from 16 to 21 November, with scheduled meetings with Theophilos III and with the Armenian patriarch Nourhan Manougian, and he is no stranger to the matter: he was nuncio in Armenia, Georgia and Azerbaijan and taught patrology, Armenian language and literature at the Oriental.

The picture he describes explains the concern. Since May 2025 Prime Minister Pashinyan has repeatedly called for Karekin II’s departure and has publicly questioned his legitimacy; Archbishops Mikael Ajapahyan and Bagrat Galstanyan have been detained or prosecuted; in February 2026 criminal proceedings were opened against the Catholicos and six members of the Supreme Spiritual Council for alleged obstruction of a judicial decision, with a ban on leaving the country. And the hardest datum is documentary: the government program for 2026-2031 lists as an official objective the removal of the current Catholicos, with an interim leader, a new statute and the election of a successor, and a report of 24 September, drawn up on Pashinyan’s instructions, details the process in five phases. The government maintains that the reform must follow the Church’s procedures and respect its canonical autonomy, which, as the medium points out, sits ill with a program that sets removal as the goal.

Amaras, and the history being rewritten

Vik van Brantegem reports that on 18 November representatives of the Christian Udi community of Azerbaijan visited the monastery of Amaras in Artsakh, prayed there in their language, lit candles and celebrated rites, and that the Azerbaijani agency APA presented the complex as an important religious and episcopal center of ancient Caucasian Albania without mentioning its Armenian history. The vice-president of the community, Rafiq Danakari, went beyond the religious celebration and claimed the monastery as the heritage of ancestors belonging to the Azerbaijani people. It was their first visit to Amaras; previously they had been to other complexes, including Dadivank, which they call Khudavang.

The history that is omitted is reconstructed by the article itself with the documentation of Monument Watch, and it is one that does not admit much discussion: according to Faustus of Byzantium, a fifth-century Armenian historian, St. Gregory the Illuminator founded there at the beginning of the fourth century the church that would become the monastery; around 406 St. Mesrop Mashtots, the inventor of the Armenian alphabet, opened in Amaras the first school that used it. It was sacked by Persians, Arabs and Mongols, was gravely damaged in the invasion of Tamerlane in 1387, and the present buildings date from the seventeenth and nineteenth centuries. For centuries it was the seat of the Catholicosate of Aghvank, and it is the burial place of St. Grigoris, grandson of Gregory the Illuminator and catholicos of the Church of Caucasian Albania, martyred while preaching there: his tomb is under the apse of the present church, rebuilt in 1858 with the support of the Armenians of Shushi. The inscriptions of the complex, with memorials of ecclesiastics, benefactors and restorations, are the epigraphic proof of that continuity.

And here comes the datum that forces us to look inward. The same article recalls that in April 2025 a congress on Christianity in Azerbaijan was held at the Pontifical Gregorian University in which Amaras, Gandzasar and Dadivank were redirected to the heritage of Caucasian Albania. That is: the thesis that the European Parliament qualified as falsification of history in its resolution of 10 March 2022—the same one that recalled the announcement of the then Azerbaijani Minister of Culture, Anar Karimov, of a working group to remove what he called fictitious Armenian traces from religious buildings—was presented in a pontifical lecture hall in Rome.

The other half of the article is the third anniversary of the order of the International Court of Justice of 17 November 2023, issued in the proceedings of Armenia v. Azerbaijan under the Convention against Racial Discrimination: it obliges Baku to guarantee those who left Nagorno-Karabakh after 19 September 2023 and wish to return a safe, unimpeded and prompt return; that those who remained may leave under the same conditions; to protect from force and intimidation those who remain or return; and to preserve identity, registration and property documents. These are binding provisional measures, not a judgment on the merits. The exodus that followed the September 2023 offensive affected more than one hundred thousand Armenians according to United Nations data cited by the Court itself, and Hovik Avanesov, defender of the cultural heritage of Artsakh, denounces that the guarantees have not been applied and calls for independent monitoring, even by satellite, and documentation of property claims: housing and work assistance in Armenia, he says, does not replace the right of return. What he also asks for, the re-establishment of an Armenian statehood in Artsakh, goes beyond what the order provides, and the article itself points this out. There is a precedent not to be lost: on 7 December 2021 the same Court had already obliged Azerbaijan to prevent and punish acts of vandalism and desecration against Armenian cultural heritage, including churches, places of worship, monuments and cemeteries.

Caritas, Coatnet and twenty-five years against trafficking

The Pope received yesterday in the Clementine Hall some forty representatives of religious organizations, civil society and international bodies gathered in Rome from 17 to 19 November on “Towards a world free from human trafficking,” with Cardinal Tarcisio Isao Kikuchi, president of Caritas Internationalis, at his side. Present were the Order of Malta, the Santa Marta Group and Talitha Kum, and the meeting marked the twenty-fifth anniversary of Coatnet, the Christian network of more than thirty organizations against trafficking. He told them that volunteers are “hands of God” that reach the abandoned and lift up the fallen, asked for leaders who are “competent and responsible,” willing to “render an account of their work” and at the same time humble and close, and asked them to respond “with courage to despair” by being instruments of a peace that is “unarmed and disarming.” He also spoke of his years of mission in Peru and of having seen there firsthand the Church present where marginalization and poverty are general.

Shalom turns forty-five

Also yesterday, in the Paul VI Hall, he received the Catholic Community Shalom, gathered in Rome and Assisi for its forty-fifth anniversary with the theme “Peace be with you”. The argument he gave them is not minor and is worth more than them: that shalom is not exhausted in social action, that peace is first a spiritual experience of reconciliation and consolation, and that Jesus is “our peace.” He acknowledged that they evangelize by the overflow of their own conversion, with simple and direct friendship, and by wearing the tau visibly. And he set them two conditions that in a movement are not rhetorical: that accompaniment fully respect the freedom and conscience of each one, and that they maintain humility, openness to change and a mature sense of belonging to the Church, cooperating with her pastors. Of the young people he said they are not those of the eighties but that their deep longings have not changed, and that forming them is “a vast field of mission.”

Six thousand young people from Lazio, on Saturday

Tomorrow, Saturday the 21st, in the Paul VI Hall, more than six thousand young people from all of Lazio will meet with the Pope in a regional youth day organized by the youth pastoral commission of the Episcopal Conference of Lazio, with an eye on the WYD in Seoul in 2027 and its motto “Confidite, Ego Vici Mundum!”. The script has been published: reception of the dioceses at eight-thirty, prayer on the Second Letter to Timothy at a quarter to ten, guided by Bishop Mauro Parmeggiani and with eight testimonies, and at eleven-thirty the greeting of Cardinal Baldassare Reina and five questions from the young people that the Pope will answer, before the renewal of baptismal promises. Parmeggiani hopes it will be “a great stimulus to embrace the vocation that God gives us.”

Simoni: the golden florin and the exorcism of Leo XIII

The mayor of Florence, Sara Funaro, yesterday presented the golden florin, the city’s highest distinction, to Cardinal Ernest Simoni in the Palazzo Vecchio, with a citation that calls him a “living martyr”. He is ninety-seven, born on 18 October 1928 in Troshan, in northern Albania, and Hoxha’s regime kept him twenty-eight years between prison and forced labor for being a Catholic priest. He lives in Florence, where he has spent the ten years of his cardinalate, and the distinction honors his seventy years of ordination. He said he is there as a “messenger of peace” and that the prize “is a great joy, it is spiritual elevation.” Archbishop Gherardo Gambelli recalled that it was Pope Francis who called him a living martyr, and compared him to Mandela.

On 17 November, after a Mass in the sanctuary of San Pio of Pietrelcina in San Giovanni Rotondo, the cardinal recited in Latin the Exorcismus in Satanam et Angelos Apostaticos published under Leo XIII, and in the broadcast of Padre Pio TV shouts and background sounds were heard, which the piece places at minute 59:48. That is what is on record. What is not on record is the origin of those sounds, and there is no pronouncement from the sanctuary or from any ecclesiastical authority. Simoni himself said of the text that it is “the most powerful prayer for peace and to eliminate all satanic forces,” and he had already recited it on 25 October last year in St. Peter’s, after a Mass presided over by Cardinal Burke, without anything similar being recorded then. The verifiable fact is that a ninety-seven-year-old cardinal prays a public nineteenth-century exorcism and that a channel broadcasts it; the background shouts make one understand that Latin bothers the demons.

The tree, the crib and the sick children

The tree in St. Peter’s Square will be lit on 7 December at the same time as the one in Gubbio, and it will be lit by children. It will be decorated by sick children, with clay ornaments made by them and fifty thousand LED lights, and the crib this year comes from Abruzzo. The fir is the one from Basilicata we reported the day before yesterday: the one from Pollino. The detail that the lighting is simultaneous with Gubbio, which boasts the largest tree in the world painted on a hillside, is appreciated.

One hundred cyclists, on Monday

On Monday the 23rd in the morning the Pope receives the world of cycling: a hundred figures from the five continents, convened by the Dicastery for Culture and Education with the International Cycling Union, among them Eddy Merckx, Bernard Hinault, Greg LeMond, Miguel Indurain, Vincenzo Nibali, Demi Vollering, Annemiek van Vleuten and Elisa Longo Borghini, plus federation officials and the organizers of the three grand tours. The audience is anchored in the Pope’s letter on sport, La vita in abbondanza; the president of the UCI, David Lappartient, has recalled the ancient links between cycling and the Church, including the passage of the Giro through the Vatican in the Jubilee, and at the end the UCI will symbolically hand over some bicycles to Caritas Rome. Athletica Vaticana has organized the donation.

The Peruvian queue: the gifts, the papacopter and a vice-commander with a wife from Chiclayo

Infobae inventories what the Pope left in Peru, and the inventory says quite a lot about the trip: a Golden Rose to Our Lady of Peace in Chiclayo and another to the Virgin Queen of Bethlehem, the Mamacha Belén, in Saqsaywaman; a shroud with his coat of arms to cover the Lord of the Earthquakes in Cusco, of whom he said at the Angelus that he wants to be “the Pope’s caress for a people that knows how to suffer with dignity and with Christian hope”; a sculpture of “Mary, the Good Mother” to the rector of the Catholic University Santo Toribio de Mogrovejo on 13 November, with a handwritten dedication in the visitors’ book; rosaries brought from the Vatican for each sister of the Little Sisters of the Abandoned Elderly of Callao and a picture of the Good Shepherd; a chalice for the vicariate of Pucallpa; and a gilded chalice and a picture to Cardinal Carlos Castillo at the farewell. They returned to him a chalice and paten of mahogany, walnut, cedar and congona made by the young people of the Don Bosco Artisans School inspired by the mokawas.

Commanders Gino Burgos and Javier Rojas recounted on RPP the flight from Chiclayo to Cajamarca: about forty-five minutes; the Pope asked to go to the cockpit as soon as they took off and was there for an hour and twenty minutes between the outbound and return legs, asked about the systems and instruments and identified from the air towns and districts that did not even appear on the crew’s maps. Both had participated in the operation for Pope Francis’s visit in 2018. The interesting detail, which is not anecdotal: he traveled with medical equipment from the Vatican because of the altitude and his recent lung operation, and the crew carried a combat paramedic.

And Lieutenant Colonel Loïc Marc Rossier, vice-commander of the Swiss Guard and chief of staff, born in Sitten, in Valais, on 23 August 1990, has a Peruvian wife and a daughter whom the Pope himself baptized in January, at the Mass of the Baptism of the Lord. Father Daniel Wachowiak tells it: “he has a Peruvian wife and his profession is the direct protection of the Pontiff.”

Of what was signed during the visit there remains a joint declaration, “Growing in the era of artificial intelligence,” between the Peruvian Ministry of Education, Scholas Occurrentes and the Inter-American Development Bank, for a pilot plan in secondary school on human capacities, mental health and the meaning of life in the face of artificial intelligence. Signed by Minister José Antonio Chang Escobedo, Martina Amengual for Scholas and Matilde Bordón for the IDB. There are no dates or figures, and Scholas is the creature of Pope Francis. Last week we reported the Roman hackathon on artificial intelligence and parish life inspired by Magnifica humanitas; the matter is on its way to becoming a line of the pontificate.

The Argentine Senate and the “Leo XIV effect”

The Argentine Senate unanimously approved on Thursday a new framework for the comprehensive care of persons with disabilities, and the dispatch titles it the “Leo XIV effect” because it comes a few days after the Pope’s visit to a home for persons with disabilities in Buenos Aires. The datum is the unanimity; the attribution is the medium’s, which cites no legislator or established authority establishing the connection, and the text also gives neither the number nor the content of the law.

Shenzhen, and the Church that is not on the paper

Trump, Xi and Putin met yesterday for ninety minutes at the Kylin Villa in Shenzhen, on the margins of APEC, and Xinhua and the Kremlin published a four-point text: reform of the UN, increase in the production and supply of petroleum derivatives, a paragraph on immunities and on the International Criminal Court not abusing its jurisdiction, and the repetition that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought. The White House issued no communiqué of its own; the text binds nothing and does not mention Ukraine or the conflict with Iran; none of the three recognizes the International Criminal Court, which issued an arrest warrant against Putin in March 2023; and there is not a single commitment to reduce arsenals, after New START expired in February.

Federico Punzi deflates it: “trilateral does not mean tripolar”. Nothing of a new Yalta: two days versus the eight of 1945, Xi seating Putin far from the table where he and Trump were, and beneath it a cold war 2.0 over energy, rare earths and artificial intelligence. Xi asked the great powers to “cooperate and not compete” and to “abandon the Cold War mentality,” and spoke of a world without nuclear weapons, “totally prohibited and destroyed”; Trump replied that expecting the United States and Russia to renounce their warheads is not realistic. Jared Kushner is said to have said that Trump does not want a unilateral peace but an agreement with Kiev and the Europeans, and that Moscow accepted entering a format with them.

And this is better read from the Church than from geopolitics, because the three who sign are exactly the three states that have on the table the three major dossiers of this pontificate. China, with the Provisional Agreement that the day before yesterday gave its twentieth bishop, the one of Xiamen. Russia, with the war and with the Patriarchate of Moscow. And the United States, which is where the fourth of the Obolo and the network of donors the Pope received on Wednesday come from. On all three fronts the Holy See has no tool other than the word: it does not sign, does not veto and has no army. On Tuesday Parolin asked at COP31 for a cohesive multilateralism and complained of geopolitical tensions guided by “petty personal interests”; three days later they announce that they will reform the UN.

Kirill turns eighty

The Orthodox magazine Foma recalls that Patriarch Kirill of Moscow turns eighty today, 20 November: son of a priest, he took the monastic habit at twenty-two, was consecrated bishop at twenty-nine and in January 2009 a local council elected him Patriarch of Moscow and All Russia. From him it collects his own description of the patriarchate as a heavy cross, and the congratulations are signed by the editorial staff; there is no trace of an official celebration. The date falls the day after Putin signed a paper on peace in Shenzhen, and the coincidence is not ours, it is the calendar’s. Of Kirill one must say what there is: he has publicly supported the invasion of Ukraine, and Pope Francis reproached him publicly in an interview in May 2022 with a phrase that has not been forgotten, that a patriarch cannot become “Putin’s altar boy.” The man who provided religious cover for a war turns eighty, and he does so without his own press having a celebration to report.

Greta laughs, and says what the climate was for

La Nuova Bussola Quotidiana devotes its editorial of 19 November to the twenty-six seconds of video in which Greta Thunberg laughs out loud when the interviewer tells her that at that moment there is a Fridays for Future demonstration in Berlin: “Really? They still do that?”. The clip comes from the documentary On Tanks into the Climate Crisis — How Activism Is Criminalised and has gone viral because it clashes with the tone of her own intervention at COP31 in Antalya, which ends today, where she said that “no one is coming to save us.”

But what matters is in the same interview, asked about the criticisms she receives—“they say we are friends of terrorists and want to bring down capitalism”—she answers herself: “yes, we do, from day one, bring down capitalism.” The climate is a pretext for a broader package, and green communism is distinguished from red in that the latter promised to produce more than capitalism and the former considers that producing is in itself an evil, whence degrowth.

And what concerns us is the discomfort, because at that same COP31 Cardinal Parolin this week defended the position of the Holy See as “a question of social, economic and anthropological justice” and, for believers, a “theological requirement”. The Holy See does not hold what it holds for Thunberg’s reasons, and Pope Francis wrote in Laudate Deum those words about the “disparaging and irrational opinions” he found within the Catholic Church itself, which we reported on Wednesday. But one must not play the distracted one: when the best-known spokesperson of the cause says that the objective was another from the first day, the one who has to explain himself better is not the one who distrusts, it is the one who defends the same thing for opposite motives.

Corrado Augias has died

Tommaso Scandroglio signs an obituary against the grain of Corrado Augias, who died on 19 November at ninety-one, who began at Rai in 1960 and at Repubblica in 1976. He maintains that the praises, including those of some Catholics, are out of place, and reproaches him for having treated faith as myth and for having reinterpreted Revelation according to his own feeling; the phrase one is left with is the one about the method, “Augias was in reality interviewing himself.” The piece also mentions that he had spoken of choosing his own death and that in a recent interview he said he would ask a trusted doctor to end his life, and the text itself does not affirm that this occurred; we leave it exactly there. For us, who shared almost nothing of what he wrote about the Church, the news is that a man has died and that we must pray for him.

“It is written: my house shall be a house of prayer; but you have made it a den of robbers”

Have a good day.
